JOHN DENVIL (JACK) JOHNSON, the leader of the Lion line, is starting his fifth
season as a tackle for Detroit. Jack and Detroit made their professional football debut
simultancously. He came here from University of Utah in 1934, the year the National
Football League franchise was transferred from Portsmouth, O. One of the greatest defensive
tackles in football history, Jack can impart his knowledge as well as use it. He coaches the
line for Dutch Clark. Johnson will be 29 in November, is married and a member of the
Church of Latter Day Saints. When not playing football Jack ranches at his home mailing
point, Grantsville, Utah. On the pro footbali fields his six-fect-three frame and 220 pounds
of brawn are as much a landmark as the Mormon temple in Salt Lake City.
PAUL (SOCKO) SZAKASH, husky fullback, was born in Chicago May 5, 1914 and still
calls the Windy City home. He played fullback for the University of Montana and blocked
so well for Milton Popovich, a halfback on the same team that Popovich was the talk of
Heavy legged, long bodied, Socko's hard running and spirited blocking won Coach Dutch
Clark's notice the moment he hit camp. He is exactly six feet tall, weighs 215 pounds and

under Glenn S. (Pop) Warner in 1932. He joined up with George "Potsy" Clark at Ports-

• He liked it so well he has remained
in the game ever since and today captains the Detroit Lions, whom he helped to popularize.
Fleetest right halfback in the game, Caddel has had to resist Hollywood offers because of
his pho:ographic qualities. He is one of handsomest males extant, in or out of football
togs. At least, his wife, Nell and six-months-old daughter think so. Caddel is now 27 years
of age. He was born in Granite, Oklahoma, but his parental home is in Tulare, Calif. His
EDWARD L. KLEWICKI, of the Hamtramck Klewikis is the original "One-Man Gang".
Ed starred at end for Coach Charley Bachman at Michigan State College for three years and
joined up with the Lions in 1936 where he immediately filled the bill. Coach Dutch Clark
rates him unequalled as a defensive end, not even excepting famed Bill Hewitt, now of the
At Cranbrook, the chief topic of conversation among the freshman candidates was
Klewicki and how to block him. One of them asked Coach Clark. Dutch replied,
me, I never blocked him. Thank heaven."
Klewicki is 27, Polish and married. He is interested in chemistry and will devote all his
time to the automobile industry when his playing days are over.
RAYMOND J. (BUTCH) MORSE is starting his fourth season at end for the Lions.
From his home city of Portland, Oregon, Morse entered Oregon University and made a
name for himself on the Pacific Coast as a fullback as well as end. His six-foot-two frame
and 206 pounds made him a natural end in pro football and that is where he has played.
Before reporting to the Lions in 1935, Butch coached Mejii University in Japan during
helped to introduce football in Nippon. Morse will be 27 in
December, is a member of Beta Theta Pi fraternity and sells insurance for a living.
GEORGE WASHINGTON (BIG CHRIS) CHRISTENSEN, now is a Detroiter by
marriage as well as adoption. He induced Miss Wilma Kerwin to become Mrs. Christensen
on June 1. He has the distinction of being the biggest as well as the oldest player in point
of service on the Lions' roster. Although the bridegroom is only 29, he played three years
at Portsmouth, O. and is starting his fifth season in Detroit.
The big tackle was handicapped last year by starting in mid-season. This year he started
with the rest from taw and his 250 pounds are honest muscle, topped with one of the
craftiest brains in football. Coach Dutch Clark rates him one of the ablest offensive tackles
the game has produced. He won his college spurs at Oregon and Portland, Oregon is his
parental home. He is one of the three men elected this year as a field leader. The others are
Vice-President, Chicago, Duluth & Georgian Bay Transit Co.

LLOYD R. (CYCLONE) CARDWELL, whirled out of his native Nebraska in 1937 to
win himself a job in the Lions' backfield. Playing right halfback for Nebraska he laid waste
some of the best teams in the Big Ten, Big Six as well as non-numerical defenses of various
Cardwell, at 25, has his best years of professional football ahead. He was hampered some-
what in his debut by an injured knee, but reported this year sound and rarin' to go. Breezy
as a prairie wind, a natural mimic, Cardwell is as much a favorite with his team mates as
ALEXANDER FRANCIS (WOJIE) WOJCIECHOWICZ was All-American center
for Coach Jimmy Crowley's Fordham eleven for two years before he signed a Lion contract
chis year to make his professional debut. Wojie was Coach Dutch Clark's first choice in the
annual draft. The East thought so much of him he was the first man signed up to play in
the Eastern All-College Stars vs. New York Giants game in the Polo Grounds. Wojie made
three round-trip airplane trips between here and New York in order to learn signals under
both Andy Kerr and Coach Clark. He is 23 years old, six feet tall and weighs an even 200
pounds. Wojie is married and his biggest thrill, next to signing a Lion contract, was
announcing the birth of Alexander Francis Wojciechowicz, Jr., born Aug. 19, 1938.
WILLIAM L. (BILL) SHEPHERD came to the Lions via Western Maryland College
with a brief stop-over at Boston. Bill played part of the 1935 season with the Boston Red-
skins after attracting notice as a member of the College All-Star team which met Chicago
Bears in Chicago before the league schedules started.
Shepherd is 27, married and the father of two husky sons. Although he is only 5 feet,
nine inches tall, Bill packs 205 pounds on his sturdy legs. He is one of the hardest men in
football to tackle, a first rate passer and kicker. He can play quarterback or fullback and
do a stint at blocking when called upon, the handy man of the backfield.
MAURICE PATT is the Hank Greenberg of the Lions, a Jewish athlete who by the appli-
cation of intelligence, ambition and determination has won himself a high place in Big
Time sports. A three-sport man at Altoona high school in Pennsylvania, Patt cut his activi-
ties to football and basketball at Carnegie Tech and starred in both. He won All-America
rating at end and was captain of the Tech basketball team.
Patt is 23 years old, 6 feet, two inches tall and weighs 207 pounds. In making his profes-
sional debut he is assured a distinguished career as a Lion. He is an exceptional pass catcher
as well as a smart defensive end. As a collegian he averaged five completed passes a gamc
igainst such teams as Notre Dame, Temple, New York University, Holy Cross, Duquesne
JACK MACKENROTH, freshman center from North Dakota University can scarcely
wait until the Lions move into Briggs Stadium. Reason: He never has escaped injury in
U. of D. Stadium. As the star lineman of North Dakota he sprained an ankle, wrenched
a back in two games played there against Gus Dorais' Titans. In the annual Lions' Freshman.
Varsity game there this Fall, Jack tore a ligament in his left knee, the only major casualty.
l'hus he starts the season on crutches. But in the limited time and opportunity at his dis-
posal, the 22-year-old lineman won a place on the roster. He is the utility man of the line,
playing center, guard or tackle with equal facility and skill. He is single and makes his
iome at Minot, N. D., is six feet, two inches tall, weighs 21).
LESTER JAMES GRAHAM is a 215-pound guard from the oil fields around Tulsa,
Oklahoma. A superb blocker, Graham was an All-Missouri Valley, Conference selection
while playing for Tulsa University, He majored in business administration, intent upon
entering the oil business with his father and it required some persuasion to induce him to
quit the oil fields for the professional football fields. Now that he has made the Lions' team
he has no regrets. Graham was born at Hominy, Okla., July 1, 1916 and still calls Hominy
home. When he confessed to no nickname, Miss Rozene Richards, daughter of the Lions'
owner, promptly dubbed him "Cracker". And "Cracker" it is.

EARL (DUTCH) CLARK: Named coach of Detroit Lions 1937. National Football
League leading scorer in 1935 and '36. All-National Football League quarterback selection
6 consecutive years. Graduate Colorado College. Associated Press All-American quarterback
selection 1928. Is a member of the Phi Gamma fraternity. Universally rated best all-around
LEROY E. (ACE) GUTOWSKY is Russia's gift co professional football. The Liony
Russian born fullback entered the National League by way of Oklahoma City University
and came to the Lions in 1934 after two seasons at Portsmouth. In 1931, he was on the
roster of the New York Giants, played one practice game. Owner Tim Mara never has
forgiven himself for letting him get away.
Gutowsky is married and lives in Kingfisher, Okla, where in the oft-season he is employed
Starting his seventh season in professional football he is established as one of the game's
VERNON RICHARD HUEFMAN is a working model of what football coaches dream
abour. He is 24 years old, six feet, two inches tall and weighs 220 pounds, all of which he
can put into high gear with the speed of a sprinter. He is a kicker and a passer as well as a
great runner, the ideal triple-threat back.
Fluffman came to the Lions from the University of Indiana last year with the fines
recommendation tag, Coach Bo McMillin has on the premises. Shortage of backfield mate.
bial and injuries forced Coach Clark to use Huffman at blocking back instead of quarter-
back. This year with a wealth of backfield material Huffman
to employ his exceptional talents in his proper backfield slot. He is a graduate of Indiana law
school, will seck to pass the bar in Michigan at the end of this season.
JAMES A. (JIM) McDONALD is the third member of the Lions' triumvirate from Ohio
State. Jim is 22 years old, six feet, one inch and weighs 195. He was purchased by the Lions
rom Cleveland Rams, who obtained him from Philadelphia Eagles. Bert Bell, of the Eagles
was entitled to first choice in the annual draft meeting and McDonald was his selection.
McDonald starred in the annual All-Star game at Chicago and repeated with trimmings
in an all-star game against the Cleveland Rams in Cleveland, Sept. 2. He was captain and
quarterback of the Buckeyes last season, majored in physical education and is a member of
sigma Chi fraternity. His home is Springfield, O.
WILLIAM (BILL) RADOVICH is the "Human Depth Bomb" of the Lion line. This
§ feet, nine inch, 235-pound guard from Southern California is so much the football type
he has appeared in football pictures at three studios on the Pacific Coast-Metro-Goldwyn-
In three seasons at guard for the Trojans, Bill made virtually every all-opponents' poll and
won top rating from such coaches as Robert Zuppke, James Phelan and Elmer Layden.
Bill has an exceptionally fast charge and loves the rough going. He is 23, a member of
Sigma Chi fraternity. To gain his degree, Bill must attend one more semester at Southern
JAMES HENDERSON (MONK) MOSCRIP is one of "the laughing boys of Stanford",
the name bestowed upon the Stanford squad by an eastern sports writer who visited Palo
Alto in 1934 before the Rose Bowl game with Columbia. At left end, Monk was the most
light-hearted of all. He played in three Rose Bowl games-against Columbia in 1934,
Alabama in 1935 and Southern Methodist in 1936. He was a team mate of Tackle Bob
Reynolds who joined the Lions last season. Monk stayed away a year after winning All-
American honors in 1934 and 1935 and All-Pacific Coast selection three years in a row.
But the lure of the Lions proved too strong and he reported this Fall. Monk was born in
Adena, O., where his parents still reside, Sept. 17, 1913. He graduated from Stanford with
a bachelor of arts degree and is a member of Zeta Psi fraternity.

hides. This operation alone employed two men for three full
days. Shaving the skins to insure even thickness throughout
required another two days of hand labor.

LOUIS PETER BARLE was born, of Slovene parents, at Gilbert, Minn., June 23, 1916
and still calls it home. He is another of that growing class of "small college" players who
make the grade in the big league. He graduated last June with a B. E. degree from Minnesota
State Teachers' College at Duluth, where he played guard, tackle, end and fullback. Coach
Clark disregarded all his previous experience and converted him into a blocking back
because Barle smacks 'em with the abandon, if not the finesse, which once distinguished
Papa Lumpkin. Barle long ago outgrew his schoolboy nickname of "Fats." He is as hard as
O. KENT (RIP) RYAN is another son of Utah making his professional debur with the
Lions. He was star quarterback of the Utah State Agricultural College during the seasons
of 1934-1935 and 1936, was chosen All-Rocky Mountain Conference quarterback for those
years, All-American in 1936. After a year in Harvard, Ryan decided to cast his lot with the
Lions this year. In the annual Lions' Freshman-Varsity game he revealed enough ability to
make enthusiastic critics hail him as the logical successor of Dutch Clark. Like his coach,
Ryan is a triple threat back—an elusive runner, a fine passer and kicker. He also showed great
defensive skill. He is married and the father of a three months old son.
RICHARD LOUIS NARDI, who led the Big Ten in individual scoring last season, makes
his professional football debut as right halfback for the Lions. At Ohio State his ball toting
was a big factor in bringing the Western Conference championship to the Buckeyes. His
200 pounds are carried on a five foot, 10-inch frame but he has amazing speed and the
priceless faculty of running through holes instead of into blind alleys on a football field.
His home town is Cleveland, where he made a name for himself in three sports at Collin-
wood high school before matriculating at Ohio State. He is 22 years old and one of three
ROBERT O'DELL (HORSE) REYNOLDS is the loftiest Lion. The big Stanford tackle
is 6 feet, five inches tall, weighs 223 pounds. Reynolds went to Leland Stanford from his
home in Okmulgee, Oklahoma and played tackle so well for three years that Stanford won
Reynolds immediately became a fixture in the Lion line when he made his professional
debut last season. This season promises to be his greatest and also his last. Bob, at 24, is
eager to get started in the business world.
J. REGIS (MONTY) MONAHAN is one of three former Ohio State stars now on the
Lions' roster. From captaining the Buckeyes' great eleven in 1934, Monty came to the Lions
to plug a hole at guard. His five foot, 10-inch frame carries 220 pounds of power and
speed, to which he adds a special knack of place-kicking. He is 29.
SIDNEY P. (SID) WAGNER is another of Michigan State College's gifts to the Lions.
Although one of the smallest, but speediest and most effective guards in the National
League, Sid starts his third season in Lion livery with the knowledge that he is as good as
Sid is 25 years old, five feet, 11 inches tall and weighs 197 pounds. His home is Lansing,
Mich, and he is a member of Phi Delta Theta fraternity.
WILLIAM (BUTCH) FELDHAUS is starting his second season at guard for the Lions
He put in three years of service at guard and tackle at the University of Cincinnati befote
landing on the Lions payroll in 1937. Bill's 225 pounds of brawn make his six-toot trame
look dumpy bue he learned enough in his freshman year to develop into a fine guard
Feldhaus' enthusiasm and love of football make him a natural leader on the field. He led
the squad each day in the race to the practice field at Cranbrook and is the official pepper-
upper of the squad. Cincinnati is his home and his name is on the roster of Sigma Chi
LEE JAMES (DIXIE) STOKES, JR., came from Centenary College, of Shrevepor, La
last year to bolster center for the Lions and became a fixture. Stokes is 25 years old, a quiet,
determined hustler, who has won the respect of his teammates. He is six feet tall, weighs
When not playing football he is in the oil business at Shreveport.
CHARLES B. (CHUCK) HANNEMAN is a local boy who made good. From Grosse
Pointe, Chuck went to Michigan State Normal College at Ypsilanti where he learned
enough football to desire more of it. He tried out for the Lions in 1936 but was sent to
Springfield, O., for further seasoning. Profiting by the additional experience, Chuck returned
in 1937 to win a place on the Lions' roster. This year with one year's Big Time experience
under his belt he was able to hold his place in the face of the finest crop of recruit ends the
Lions ever mustered. In the opinion of his teammates, Chuck is headed for a great year.
TONY FRANCIS MATISI is the latest of a long line of All-American tackles and guards
turned out by Jock Sutherland, coach of Pittsburgh. Tony,
honors last season at Pittsburgh, is making his professional debut with the Lions at tackle.
He was born in New York City of Italian parents on August 23, 1914. His home is in
Endicott, New York. Tony is six feet, one inch tall, weighs 230 pounds. At Pitt, Tony com-
peted in track, wrestling and boxing as well as football. He won the intra-mural heavyweight
oxing championship at Pitt, letters in football in 1935, 1936 and 1937.
WILLIAM C. ROGERS. As a member of the fine Villanova College teams of 1935-36-37,
Rogers made an enviable reputation as a guard and tackle. Although weighing 230 pounds
he ran the 100 yards in 11½ seconds and in high school at Westboro, Massachusetts, was
fast enough to play fullback. He punts, passes, blocks and receives passes, place kicks, blocks,
nd. when shifted into the backfield on defense does a good job of pass intercepting o
nocking down. He was given honorable mention on the Associated Press. All-Faster
Rogers gained his Bachelor of Science degree from Villanova as a student of business
administration, majoring in economics. But his current intention is to become a director
FRED (CHOPPER) VANZO is one of the greatest blocking backs ever developed in the
Big Ten. He comes to the Lions from Northwestern University, via New York Giants, who
drafted him and later sold him to the Lions.
Vanzo is 22 years of age. He was born in Universal, Indiana, January 8, 1916 of American-
Austrian parentage and still lives in Universal.
